A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Poison-splat, with matching methods, experiments and identifiable appendix material. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite appendix reorganization and additions.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack experiments on NeRF-Synthetic, Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks-and-Temples, including resource measurements, black-box transfer, ablations and reconstruction visualizations.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds Mip-Splatting experiments, partial-poisoning tests, defense analyses, image-quality measurements and attacker timings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the attack objectives remain unchanged: proxy-model rendering, total-variation maximization, optional perturbation projection and proxy updates. The additional threat-model summary and disclosed iteration counts document the existing procedure.

E1.justification: The datasets and represented scenes are retained. Appendix H adds a restricted-control scenario with only 20–80% of views poisoned, mixing clean and poisoned inputs instead of poisoning every view. The added constrained Palace result uses a scene already evaluated unconstrained in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix J and Figure 7 add Gaussian-filter and bilateral-filter comparisons against no preprocessing in the defense-quality analysis; v1 examined Gaussian-count capping. The naive TV attack comparator remains unchanged. Mip-Splatting is an added victim model, rather than a competing attack.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation with a Mip-Splatting victim, randomly selected partial-poisoning subsets, a reported 2–6 million Gaussian-cap sweep, and smoothing preprocessing. It also measures poisoned-input SSIM and PSNR against clean images and separates attacker preparation and optimization time. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: The existing perturbation-strength analysis gains input-quality measurements. New appendices test dependence on poisoning fraction, resource–quality tradeoffs across defense thresholds, smoothing-induced reconstruction damage and attacker runtime. These address substantial practical questions beyond v1's proxy ablation, perturbation sweep and fixed-cap examples.

E5.justification: V1 Tables 6–7 report means and standard deviations across three runs. Their counterparts, v2 Tables 10–11, retain the cost means but omit standard deviations and the accompanying three-run statement. Table 12 uses three-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting for poisoning fractions, but broad uncertainty disclosure for the retained perturbation study is lost. This does not establish fewer experimental runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain existing values, with a constrained Palace row added to Table 3; perturbation-study cost means also match. Substantial new results include Mip-Splatting failures on all eight listed Mip-NeRF360 scenes under unconstrained attack, partial-poisoning outcomes, input-quality scores, defense tradeoffs and attacker timings. These are additional results under specified conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7, optimization definitions and Gaussian densification mathematics are retained. The structured threat-model appendix largely consolidates existing assumptions. Appendix K adds empirical timing and explanatory cost accounting without a new formal complexity derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: training-data poisoning can exploit adaptive 3DGS complexity, increase resource consumption, potentially cause denial of service and resist painless naive defenses. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 attributes Mip-Splatting memory failures to quantile computation during densification, explains difficulties with a universal Gaussian cap and discusses smoothing's loss of fine details. It also interprets poisoning-view selection and attacker–victim timing. These substantially expand the mechanism explanations and practical applicability boundaries beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the Mip-Splatting implementation reference and source location, discloses the original defense caps of 6, 4 and 2 million Gaussians, and gives T = 6000 and T-tilde = 25 for the timing example. Hardware and existing code-access information remain unchanged. The new inner/outer-iteration wording is inconsistent with those stated counts.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including Mip-Splatting, multi-scale Gaussian splatting, bilateral filtering, Unsegment Anything and DarkSAM. The positioning around training-stage availability attacks remains essentially unchanged. Scaffold-GS's citation suffix and Koh's added publication year identify existing references, not new research comparisons.

P1.justification: The main narrative, method description and conclusion remain largely verbatim. V2 expands the appendix roadmap, introduces a structured threat-model summary and reorganizes supporting sections. Limited edits include affiliations, funding acknowledgments and renaming Societal Impacts to Ethics Statement; there is no extensive rewrite of retained material.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual evidence with Mip-Splatting, poisoning-fraction, defense-threshold and timing tables. The perturbation tables gain image-quality columns and a revised structure. Figure 6 expands the earlier defense visualization, while Figure 7 adds smoothing comparisons with detail crops. Original Figures 1–5 and poisoned-image galleries are retained.

improvement.justification: V1 established large resource increases but left partial attacker control, actual training failure and attack-generation cost incompletely tested. V2 addresses these gaps through reported Mip-Splatting failures, partial-poisoning experiments and attacker timings, while quantifying distortion and defense tradeoffs. These additions substantially strengthen evidence for practical feasibility and limitations. Losing the earlier perturbation-study standard deviations and introducing inconsistent iteration wording weaken reporting, but the empirical gains outweigh those harms.
